    Recipe notes & sources

    Video baseline: 15 g coffee, 250 g water, five equal pours, a 45 s bloom and an approximate 3:00 finish. App adaptations: 1:17.5 and 1:15.5 styles, the medium-light temperature preset, and timing changes outside the original recipe. Scaled finish times are estimates, not predictions.

    Brewing notes and adaptations

    Watch the original ↗
    Set up the brewer
    • Use a V60 01 for a single cup. Hoffmann favors plastic because it is easy to warm. Rinse the paper and warm the plastic cone with hot tap water, then discard the rinse water. Give glass or ceramic a thorough preheat with boiling water, especially for light roasts.
    • Use soft, filtered brew water and a scale. A gooseneck gives you more control over a thin stream, and a regular kettle also works if you can pour steadily.
    • Start medium-fine. Lean finer for lighter coffee and coarser for darker coffee. Add the grounds, level the bed, make a shallow well in the center, and tare the scale.
    Bloom, pour, and drain
    • Start the timer with the first drops. Pour into the center and spiral outward so the whole bed gets wet. Lift the brewer slightly and give it a small swirl at about 0:10, then leave it to bloom.
    • Hold the spout close and move in slow circles over the coffee. Use roughly 5 g/s as a starting pace. A steady low stream distributes water and agitation across the bed. A prolonged center pour can dig a crater. A higher center pour that breaks the stream before it hits the bed can spread the agitation, but low circles are easier to repeat.
    • Stick to the pauses so the slurry can drop between pulses. After the last pour, gently swirl to settle the grounds, then let the bed drain. A little variation around the finish time is normal.
    Scale the recipe and dial in to taste
    • At the original ratio, 12 g uses 200 g of water in 40 g charges, 15 g uses 250 g in 50 g charges, and 18 g uses 300 g in 60 g charges. Keep each charge at about one-fifth of the total.
    • Use fresh off-boil water for light roasts, roughly 90–95 °C for medium, around 90 °C for medium-dark, and roughly 80–85 °C for dark. Retaining heat through the bloom can help a light roast taste sweeter.
    • If the brew tastes thin or sour, try a slightly finer grind first. If it tastes harsh or dries your mouth, try a bit coarser. Let taste guide your adjustments. Water quality, the coffee itself, and grind all matter alongside technique.
    • Separate cups keep the method close to the original. A combined batch uses the same water fractions with longer pours. Use a V60 that fits the dose, and expect its finish time to vary.
